item.title: Understanding How Micro-Bets Hijack Your Brain
item.description:
Dopamine

Understanding How Micro-Bets Hijack Your Brain

Discover the brain science of betting apps and how to rewire your mind to heal.

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Microgambling compresses the anticipation of winning, flooding the brain with rapid-fire dopamine hits.
  • Unpredictable rewards create an obsessive loop that mimics the addictive mechanics of a slot machine.
  • Constant dopamine surges can alter the brain's reward, executive, and emotional regulation centers.
  • Structured support and cognitive behavioral therapy can help rewire neural pathways for lasting recovery.

The modern world is moving faster than ever. Our beautiful, complex brains are constantly being bombarded by a digital feed of pings, updates, and instant gratification. Recently, this high-speed environment has collided with the world of sports betting, creating a phenomenon known as "micro-bets."

Platforms like Betr have revolutionized how we wager. They allow users to bet on micro-events, like whether the next pitch in a baseball game will be a strike or a ball. Because these bets are resolved in mere seconds, they drastically increase the frequency of wagers. This creates a fast-paced loop that closely mimics the mechanics of a slot machine.

How do we know when casual betting crosses the line? The American Psychiatric Association defines specific criteria. Key signs include:

  • The need to gamble with increasing amounts of money to achieve the desired thrill.
  • Restlessness or irritability when attempting to cut down.
  • "Chasing losses"—returning another day to get even.
  • Lying to conceal the extent of involvement.
  • Jeopardizing relationships, jobs, or educational opportunities.

If you or someone you love is caught in this cycle, I want you to know first and foremost: you are not alone, and this is not a moral failing. It is a matter of brain wiring. When we understand how our brains work, we begin to understand ourselves with deeper compassion. Let’s look at the neuroscience of microgambling, why it is so difficult to walk away, and how we can use neuroplasticity to heal.

Process Addiction and the Desert Mirage

Gambling is classified as a "process addiction" or behavioral addiction. Unlike substance abuse, the individual is not addicted to a chemical, but rather to the action itself and the physiological feeling it produces.

A powerful metaphor for this experience is a desert mirage. Imagine walking through a scorching, arid landscape, exhausted and desperately thirsty. On the horizon, you see a shimmering oasis of water. Your brain lights up with hope, relief, and anticipation.

You run toward it, expending what little energy you have left, only to arrive and find nothing but dry sand. You are left emptier and more depleted than before—yet almost immediately, another shimmering mirage appears on the horizon, and the desperate chase begins again.

This perfectly illustrates the insatiable craving and the empty void that a gambling addiction creates. With the surge of online sports betting, millions of adults are experiencing this endless chase. Microgambling apps intentionally target a highly connected population, leading to a massive surge in young adults (particularly ages 18-24) across all backgrounds. Furthermore, this accessibility has led to a growing prevalence among women and marginalized communities who might never have set foot inside a traditional casino.

The Brain on Micro-gambling

To heal, we must first understand what is happening inside our brains during the betting process. The primary neurochemical at play here is dopamine—our brain's reward and motivation messenger.

Interestingly, the massive release of dopamine actually happens during the anticipation of the outcome, not just the win. Micro-gambling compresses this anticipation phase into seconds, providing rapid-fire dopamine hits that train the brain to crave the betting process itself.

This is driven by a mechanism called "unpredictable reinforcement." Because the brain doesn't know when the win is coming, it becomes obsessed with solving the puzzle, making it incredibly difficult to stop. The anticipation of the imagined reward causes a surge of dopamine before every bet.

Over time, this dopamine flooding causes physical changes in the brain's structure and function:

  • The Ventral Striatum: The brain's reward center becomes hijacked. It requires more extreme stimuli to experience pleasure, a phenomenon known as tolerance.
  • The Prefrontal Cortex: This incredible part of the brain handles impulse control and executive function. In a gambling addict, this area shows reduced activity, making it physically harder to rationally assess risk.
  • The Amygdala: This region affects emotional regulation, leading to the severe highs and crushing lows associated with the gambling cycle that increases anxiety and depression.

Rewiring the Mind for Healing

The most beautiful thing about the human brain is its capacity to heal. Through neuroplasticity, the brain has the ability to change, adapt, and build new neural pathways. Just as it learned the addiction, it can rewire itself over time with proper support and abstinence.

If you are looking for the light at the end of the tunnel, here are compassionate, science-backed steps for rewiring the mind:

  • Practice Awareness Through CBT: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) helps restructure distorted thinking patterns. By naming your emotions and triggers, you shift the power away from the amygdala and back into the logical prefrontal cortex.
  • Find Community: Support groups like Gamblers Anonymous provide community and accountability. We are deeply social creatures, and our nervous systems regulate best when we feel connected. Support groups provide connection and meaning. Remember, shame thrives in secrecy, but empathy builds through connection.
  • Allow for Self-Compassion: Changing a behavior pattern takes time and patience. Treat yourself as you would your best friend, with love and honesty. When you approach your healing with compassion rather than harsh judgment, you create a safe internal environment for your brain to heal and develop new thinking and behaving patterns.
  • Seek Professional Support: For severe cases, specialized treatment facilities offer a safe, trigger-free environment to begin the hard work of emotional regulation.

Recovery is possible. In fact, research shows that one in three people recover from gambling addiction. Through therapy and support groups one has the power to take control of their brain, rewrite new story, and wire one's mind for true love and joy. Awareness is the first courageous step toward healing.

item.title: The Lobotomy Isn’t Dead, It Just Got Precise
item.description:
Neuroscience

The Lobotomy Isn’t Dead, It Just Got Precise

Brain surgery for mental illness still exists, but it's a lot different now.

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Classic lobotomy peaked in the 1940s and 1950s and had faded by the 1960s, as antipsychotic drugs arrived.
  • Image-guided surgery for severe, treatment-resistant OCD exists today as a distant descendant of lobotomy.
  • Modern procedures are targeted and tightly screened, but the evidence base is still small.
  • The history is a lesson in how desperation, thin evidence, and weak oversight can combine.
Source: General Kenobi/Pexels

Say "lobotomy" and most people picture a patient on a gurney, a dimly lit operating room at the end of a long, empty hallway, and a doctor holding something resembling an ice pick. Surgeons still operate on the brain to treat psychiatric illness, but things are a little different today. It isn't the lobotomy of the 1940s, but it isn't entirely unrelated either. So, are lobotomies still performed today? Sort of.

What a Lobotomy Actually Was

In late 1935, Portuguese neurologists began destroying connections between the frontal lobes and deeper brain structures in patients with severe mental illness. The 1949 Nobel Prize was awarded to one of them for this work. Walter Freeman, an American neurologist, later popularized a faster "transorbital" version that reached the brain through the eye socket, and tens of thousands of lobotomies were eventually performed.

The context matters. Asylums were overcrowded, effective treatments were scarce, and lobotomy looked like hope. It was used for schizophrenia, severe depression, OCD, and even "psychopathic personality." It was also applied unevenly. One recent historical review notes that the informal selection criteria included being female and being non-compliant.

Did It Work?

The best answer is "sort of," and mostly in the short term. In one of the early reports on 20 patients, roughly a third were described as greatly improved, a third moderately improved, and a third unchanged. But follow-up lasted only weeks. Some patients did become calmer and went home. Others became apathetic, disinhibited, or developed seizures, and some died.

By the 1960s, classic lobotomy had been largely abandoned for two main reasons: One, chlorpromazine, the first widely used antipsychotic, arrived in the U.S. in 1955. Two, the mounting ethical backlash from professionals and the general public finally reached a tipping point.

Then Versus Now

Today's descendants fall under the name psychiatric neurosurgery, and they're reserved for a very small group: people with severe OCD, for example, who haven't responded to medication and exposure therapy. The differences from the 1940s are substantial. Instead of cutting blindly, surgeons use MRI guidance to place tiny, precise lesions with focused radiation or laser heat, or they implant electrodes for deep brain stimulation (DBS), which can be adjusted. The FDA approved DBS for severe OCD in 2009 under a special pathway for rare conditions, which means it was judged to have probable benefit, not proven effectiveness.

And the results? A meta-analysis of 38 studies found that around 57 percent of patients with refractory OCD responded to either ablative surgery or DBS, with no clear difference between the two. That's meaningful for people who've run out of options, but it also means roughly four in ten didn't respond.

The studies are small, too. One recent report examined 10 patients treated with laser capsulotomy, and another study looked at six patients treated between 2017 and 2025. Researchers also note that cognitive side effects appear subtle but are not yet well studied.

Conclusion

Psychosurgery didn't vanish. It narrowed, and in doing so it traded the confidence of the 1940s for caution. The real lesson of the lobotomy era isn't that brain surgery for mental illness is inherently monstrous. It's what happens when a treatment spreads faster than the evidence for it. The open question today is how we weigh last-resort options for people who have exhausted everything else, and how we make sure the evidence keeps up.

item.title: When Something as Natural as Aging Becomes a Problem
item.description:
Aging

When Something as Natural as Aging Becomes a Problem

The business of making us dissatisfied.

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • People have every right to change their appearance. The question is how freely that wish is formed.
  • A need tied to aging can never be fully met, because aging never stops.
  • Comparing ourselves with altered images may shift what we perceive as a normal face.
  • Freedom includes the right to change our faces and the right to leave them as they are.

Personal freedom and self-determination mean that people have the right to do with their faces and bodies what pleases them. No one has the right to decide for someone else how they should look, whether they should undergo cosmetic surgery, or how they should deal with their appearance. This freedom is fundamental and should never be questioned.

But there is another question, perhaps a more important one: How freely do we make these decisions when an entire industry works tirelessly to convince us that something is wrong with the way we look?

I am not talking about promoting a healthy, active lifestyle and biopsychosocial well-being. I am addressing a 24/7 pressure to dictate how we should look like.

One of the most powerful mechanisms in modern economics is simple: Do not merely produce a product. Produce a need. Better yet, produce a need that can never be completely satisfied.

Aging is a perfect example. Aging is one of the most beautiful aspects of life. We gain experiences, learn, love, struggle, succeed, fail, and grow. Our faces and bodies document this journey. Wrinkles, changing skin, and gray hair are visible expressions of a life being lived. However, we are meant to be ashamed of them. Wrinkles are defeats, a sign that we lost the fight against Mother Nature. Interestingly, in some Middle Eastern cultures, gray hair has traditionally been associated with dignity, wisdom, and social respect. There, visible signs of aging can be regarded not as something to conceal but as something that deserves recognition.

How, then, have we transformed this natural and meaningful process into a money-printing machine? The answer is surprisingly simple: We've convinced ourselves that aging is a problem that must be corrected.

The beauty industry has made wrinkles undesirable and gray hair embarrassing. It presents the natural changes of the face as signs of neglect, loss of attractiveness, or personal failure. Then it offers an endless collection of solutions: creams, makeup, anti-aging treatments, painful injections, and cosmetic surgery.

Above all, we are expected to remain "sexy" at every age—and, of course, no one can ever be sexy enough. Forget dignity, grace, wisdom, or the beauty of a life fully lived. What matters increasingly is our ability to remain sexually attractive, as though that were the ultimate measure of our worth. We've made “looking sexy” the main purpose of life.

And here is the critical economic advantage: Aging never stops. A product that promises to eliminate the signs of aging is addressing a process that cannot be eliminated. Every temporary improvement creates the possibility of another intervention. Every new wrinkle becomes another problem to solve. The customer is entering a potentially endless cycle of dissatisfaction and correction.

From a psychological perspective, the mechanism is even more troubling. Human beings evaluate themselves partly through social comparison. We look at others to understand what is attractive, acceptable, and desirable. When the images surrounding us are increasingly youthful, digitally altered, or cosmetically modified, our perception of what is normal can change. What was once an ordinary face becomes an imperfect face. What was once a natural feature becomes something requiring treatment—and perhaps most importantly, manufactured insecurity can begin to feel like a personal preference.

We may sincerely believe that we want to look younger. But it is worth asking where that desire comes from. Would we feel the same discomfort with our wrinkles if we lived in a society that celebrated them? Would we seek the same procedures if aging were associated primarily with dignity rather than decline?

These questions do not mean to suggest that people who choose cosmetic procedures are manipulated, superficial, or incapable of making independent decisions. That would be unfair and psychologically simplistic; people have many legitimate reasons for wanting to change their appearance.

The issue is the social and economic environment in which that decision is made. There is a profound difference between offering someone the opportunity to change their appearance and systematically teaching them to dislike it: The first expands freedom while the second can undermine it.

Perhaps the greatest achievement of the anti-aging industry is its ability to convince people that looking their age is something to apologize for. But aging is not a failure of the body; it is evidence that life is continuing.

item.title: Is Trauma Forever?
item.description:
Trauma

Is Trauma Forever?

Your capacity to recover may be bigger than your pain.

Posted October 16, 2026

Source: Drs Producoes / iStock

Warren was a 28-year-old staff sergeant in the Air Force when he nearly killed a subordinate. He choked the man in a fit of rage so severe it shocked even Warren when he finally came to. He reached out to one of my students looking for help.

On the surface, Warren's issues looked familiar. Stress at work and trouble sleeping. While this was happening, his wife was pregnant with their first child and the anxiety around becoming a father sat on top of everything else. As one of my students began working with Warren to help release the negative emotions, something came to the surface that had a lot of charge.

Warren had been deployed in Afghanistan. He was in a motorcade when an IED exploded beneath the vehicle in front of him and four of his close friends died. He had avoided thinking about it for nearly a year. When it came up in session, the guilt hit hardest emotionally. My student helped him release and process that guilt and he left the session feeling better. But the next week, Warren came back angrier than ever.

It was like peeling back an onion. Underneath the combat trauma was the real root of his symptoms: a memory from when he was four. Warren's father found him playing with matches and then proceeded to grab him by the back of the neck and throw him across the room. Warren hit a bookcase and crumpled to the ground while his father kept yelling.

Warren wanted to be a good father and avoid the same behaviors he experienced as a child. He was open and willing to release the anger he felt.

When Warren released the anger and fear from that event, everything shifted. Within two weeks, he reported that his anger issues and all related symptoms were gone.

Warren's trauma was real. The pain was real. And it was not forever.

The Story

In Western society, we tend to treat trauma like an identity. Social media rewards the telling and retelling of baggage. AI is designed to keep responding to your inquiries, so it keeps on digging into your trauma and reinforcing your story. This can lead to emotional rumination and that makes you feel worse and worse.

We have been so trained through talk shows, reality TV, and social media that drama is part of life. We expect change to be dramatic. We expect healing to take years. And when it does not look like it does on TV or how others do it, we question whether it was real.

That expectation is the problem. When someone loops through the same painful story without resolution, they are not processing it, they're rehearsing it. The emotional charge stays locked in place and the belief hardens: This is who I am now.

What the Research Actually Shows

Many people exposed to traumatic events do not develop chronic PTSD. That fact surprises most people because we focus almost entirely on the people who struggle longest. And we put them in the spotlight. However, resilience after adversity is not the exception but the most common outcome. Our capacity to recover is a feature of being human.

A student of mine once volunteered for a demonstration at a live event. His issue disappeared so quickly that he said, "That was too easy. I should have at least cried." All I could say was, "I'm sorry it was so easy and so drama-free."

Change does not need to be dramatic, and it doesn’t need to take years. The nervous system can shift old emotional programming when given the right conditions to do so. What matters is that the process reaches the root of the problem where the emotional charge was installed.

Release Can Create Forgiveness

Warren had to release the anger and fear his father installed in him at age four. A former teacher I worked with, a woman who had survived a school shooting, had to release the guilt and terror from that day.

In both cases, the release came first, and the forgiveness followed. When the emotional charge simply left, what remained was the learning without the pain.

The teacher smiled after her release and said, "I am alive, and I had helped as many children as I could." The event was still tragic. But the baggage was gone.

You can't push yourself into forgiveness but it becomes possible once the emotional baggage releases. The internal or external work of releasing old patterns and baggage is an act of forgiveness toward the self and others.

Two Questions for Seeing if It’s Baggage

1. When you think about a painful event, ask whether the emotional charge you feel right now is proportionate to what is happening in this moment, or whether it belongs to the original event. Baggage and present-moment emotion feel different once you learn to tell them apart. Baggage fires at full intensity even when the current situation does not warrant it.

2. Notice whether you are moving through the event or circling it. Processing has a direction. It leads somewhere. Rehearsal loops back to the same place every time. If you have been telling yourself the same story with the same charge for months or years, you are stuck in the loop.

Recovery is a process. Since your nervous system learned that negative programming, it can learn new programming. The capacity to release old emotional patterns is built into you.

item.title: Remembering Salem at Halloween
item.description:
Magical Thinking

Remembering Salem at Halloween

Current revelry and revolting history.

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Witches, once feared and even publicly hanged or burned, now are figures of fun at Halloween.
  • War, disease, scarcity, and religious zeal formed the backdrop to Salem’s witch-hunt.
  • As science advances, superstition retreats.

This Halloween season found us in a small lakeside town in Northern Michigan for a warm October “Witches Night Out” festivity, where costumed revelers, four out of five of them women, commandeered its main street.

Shops decorated for the occasion rewarded visitors with Jell-O shots and squirting syringes filled generously with spiced rum. Gloom is glitz at Halloween. A bright red-headed witch in a sparkling green dress recalling the Bette Midler character in The Witches of Eastwick patrolled the sidewalk. Then there was a Maleficent; a Cat-Woman; a Wicked Witch of the West, a blue-eyed Celtic Princess or two, and an assortment of Goths done up in peaked hats, special-effects contact lenses, black eye-shadow, spider-web stockings, and sequined high-heeled boots.

The author, persuaded to wear a “fascinator” unconvincingly, joined Halloween celebrants in Elk Rapids, Michigan.
Source: Photo Courtesy, Christine Narum Eberle (2025).

Fear as Fun

Was the evening ghastly and macabre? A night for roaming, mournful, unrequited souls? No. On Halloween, fear is fun. The vibe that night was “witchy,” “funny,” “creepy-cute,” and “spooky,” so said the participants.

Or to put it another way, Halloween is playful. Safe, too, it should be noted, because of all the 365 nights of the year, Halloween is the safest. Parents are out on the sidewalk supervising.

Halloween is popular. In the United States and Canada, Halloween falls only behind Christmas in holiday sales revenue. Celebrants spend billions on decorative outdoor ghosts and skeletons, costume horror-pop culture parties, and candy and wine.

If there was a spirit on the loose this gleeful night in small-town Michigan, it was a community spirit: bipartisan, commercialized, frisky, secular, boozy, performative, and modern.

A Demon-Haunted Colony

We tend to think of our nation’s history as an ascending achievement pushing onward: colonists striving for freedom established a beachhead where opportunity stretched ahead and wherein democracy, a radical, modern notion, could take root and flourish. This was the “new world.” America was the future. Society would be reinvented.

Those Founding Fathers that we know best now two hundred fifty years later were thinkers of the European Enlightenment installed here in the American outpost. For Benjamin Franklin a scientist and a tinkerer, the world could be known and explained. For Thomas Jefferson, a political thinker and a visionary, a government free from ancient constraints could aspire to perfection. James Madison believed that governmental authority arose from the will of the people. Thomas Paine and Ethan Allen inveighed against superstition.

Three generations before in Puritan New England, three-and-a-third centuries ago, however, colonists, religious dissenters, and still very much medieval people, could never have sanitized the scary as we do today.

Puritan theologians took “the supernatural” with dead, medieval seriousness. Halloween was “All Hallows Eve,” the night before “All Saints Day,” both somber observances, remembrances of the dead. Local ministries condemned folk-celebrations of the days as “abominable shame” and forbade them because they risked summoning demonic influences.

For Cotton Mather, the most powerful Puritan theologian and a zealous booster of witch trials, the “heart-breaking exercises,” remnants of Catholic paganism and near witchcraft, comprised a grievous threat to the Puritan errand into the “wilderness.” And by “wilderness,” Puritan colonists meant not just the forest yet to be cleared, but a haunted place that lay dangerously nearby, a “howling demonized space” as one historian described it.

Colonists in Massachusetts Bay would build a shining “city upon a hill,” an example for all the world to behold. Their errand was not only aspirational. “There is no land in the Universe,” Mather declared grandiosely in his defense of Salem’s deadly witch trials, “more free from the debauching and debasing Vices of Ungodliness.” In this righteous, driven society, “Swearing, Sabbath-breaking, Whoring, Drunkenness, and the like,” he proclaimed, “do not make a Gentleman, but a Monster, and a Goblin.” Virtue tempted Satan. “Where [else] would the Devil show most malice?” Cotton Mather asked, if not in the place of “serious piety,” that most challenged his evil sway.

A Society Deeply Stressed

It may be hard to imagine that the eventual twentieth-century superpower would have held on so tenuously in the seventeenth. But the American colonies faced several real compounding threats. Settlers quarreled over grazing rights. Epidemics periodically ravaged the colonies. Low level territorial strife with native populations burst into two fierce wars, one of which destroyed half of New England’s colonial villages. Crop failures brought near starvation. Harsh winters nearly froze the venture out. And the wet springs that followed likely poisoned stored rye with the fungus that produces the hallucinogen, ergot. (Among other symptoms more severe, ergot poisoning causes convulsions and delirium.)

It is unsurprising that a culture so beset, traumatized, tightly wound, and eager to indulge its religious fanaticism would turn paranoid. A fearful mood comprises the psychological background of the infamous witch-hunt that accused 200 Salem colonists. Most of them were women.

Accusation and Public Execution

I will elaborate more in a follow-up “Play in Mind” piece, but for now, here is the story. In January 1692, two girls ages 9 and 11 began to suffer seizures and fits of screaming. Three more soon joined in. Within a month, a local doctor had diagnosed demonic possession. Shortly after, religious authorities with legal authority began to finger culprits, alleging witchcraft. Panic spread as local magistrates examined suspects, convicting 30. By early summer, Bridget Bishop became the first to be hanged on the strength of “spectral evidence.” (Say her name…) Eighteen more, again mostly women, followed her to the gallows. At least five more died in filthy prison cells. One more man died under torture.

Before long, regret began to settle in. Accusers recanted their testimonies. Judges begged forgiveness. Robert Calef, who had corresponded with Cotton Mather and other ministers during the trials, denounced the “Biggotted Zeal, stirring up a Blind and most Bloody rage.”

The Tide Turns

By 1700, the era that came to be called the “Age of Enlightenment” was well underway. Science began to advance where superstition retreated. History is complicated and nuanced. And sometimes deeply ironic. In his later years, Cotton Mather, also a naturalist, patiently gathered evidence and became an advocate for vaccination against recurrent smallpox plagues. We may rightly see him as a transitional figure between the medieval and the modern.

Now not incidentally, three-and-a-century later, party witches are free to paint their faces green to join celebrations that tame the scary and poke fun at the demonic.

item.title: Learning How to Trust Again Without Second-Guessing Yourself
item.description:
Trust

Learning How to Trust Again Without Second-Guessing Yourself

Three approaches to trust and how they can benefit decision-making

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Relating to others based on goodwill trust can improve human experience.
  • Trusting others based on skills encourages a higher quality of work.
  • Being known as a habitual latecomer or another flaw does not mean you cannot be trusted in other areas.
Source: Vitaly-gariev / Unsplash

In this information age, trusting the capabilities of artificial intelligence is becoming more common than ever. Understandably, AI is becoming a regular part of clinical practice as psychologists are weaving it into their administrative routines and reporting a clearer understanding of its risks and benefits.

In the case of information sharing—imagine telling a colleague about current events while they are busy surfing the internet to verify what you are telling them. Obviously, trusting the capabilities of AI has its place in society. However, people trusting each other can never be overemphasized. It is all about striking a balance and asking open-ended questions to gain insights from multiple sources in your interactions with machine learning.

You have heard the phrases, “I don’t trust him,” “I don’t trust her,” “I don’t trust them,” or “I don’t trust it.” These conversations could happen at work, in a social setting, or in intimate relationships. With such a bold claim, you might ask, “What types of trust are you referring to?” Because trust is not one-size-fits-all. Trust is not an all-or-nothing type of arrangement. Trust, in effect, has different types and layers. Before you use the phrase, “I don’t trust…,” consider this:

Source: Jose Aljovin / Unsplash

There are several relational types of trust. As you go about your merry way every day, you run into different settings that require you to trust or not trust, be it a person, place, or thing. But you are constantly negotiating during different encounters.

Most of the time, you subconsciously authorize a person, place, or thing to serve your purpose. For example, when stopped at a traffic light and it turns green, you subconsciously trust that the intersection is safe to cautiously proceed. You trust that the traffic light is letting you go while the rest of the drivers in their vehicles wait for their turn to proceed.

You walk into your place of work trusting the integrity of the building not to collapse on you. You showed up at the front desk and were asked to sit and wait for the interviewer to call you in for the job interview. While sitting, you trusted the integrity of the chair to hold your weight. You walked into a doctor’s office hoping to be attended to and trusting the physician to take care of your health. These are several trust-related examples that show how you do things without even thinking about the trust quotient.

There are three types of trust that serve as the premise of this article, which explores how they are applied in different areas of work, social interactions, and relationships.

Relating with others based on goodwill trust

This type of trust is based on mutual expectations of open commitment to each other. There is an innate familiarity that exists when you come in contact with another person, irrespective of demographic characteristics. That is why people co-exist in communities, including co-existing with their pets and livestock.

Incidentally, that level of co-existence does not generally exist between wild animals and humans. People are generally afraid of lions, tigers, alligators, pythons, etc., because of their wild nature, and people respect their habitats for humanitarian purposes. The understanding of such co-existence generates goodwill trust to be kind and compassionate, and to look out for one another. Without goodwill trust, co-existence issues arise. It is from basic goodwill trust that people do business together or even agree to disagree.

Contractual trust

This type of trust focuses on written or oral agreement. People can hardly work together without agreeing. Such agreement occurs either verbally, via handshakes, or in written form. In the midst of agreement lies the trust that people will do as they said.

This level of trust is what moves friendships, relationships, and businesses forward, especially when it comes to employers and their team members. Initial exchanges can take place in electronically signing a document, over the phone, or through in-person interactions. Contractual trust defines expectations between two parties. Understanding the nature of this type of trust lays the foundation for skills-based trust, which is also known as competence trust.

Competence trust

This is a type of trust that is based on skills. The majority of people go to their doctors based on the physician’s medical competence. In other words, you may not need to know your physician’s social life for you to allow them to treat you.

The skills type of trust depends heavily on their years of training in a particular area. For example, a landscaper who mows your lawn does so based on their area of training. A coach who coaches a team does so based on their expertise. A registered nurse cares for their patients based on their clinical training. An attorney represents their clients in court based on legal competence. Interestingly, people are willing to authorize others to serve them once they establish mutual trust. Simply put, competence-based trust demands a high level of commitment and professionalism that is not necessarily required on a personal level.

Source: Michael Smith / Unsplash

On a personal note, I have had my landscaper for more than 20 years. He does his job exceptionally well. In fact, he has a passion for taking care of grass and doing yard work. But in those 20 years of our business relationship, he is always late—sometimes by hours and sometimes by days.

At the beginning of our business together, I realized that he’s not good at time management. I had to make an executive decision about whether to discharge him of his duties because of his tardiness or to retain him for his ability to pay attention to details when taking care of my yard. You’ll find similar examples apply in other areas.

A physician can be great in treating their patients but can be anti-social outside of work; a comedian can entertain their audiences on a contractual basis yet be an introvert when they’re not working. Categorically, one can be good and trusted in one aspect, and yet unreliable in another area.

Understanding this concept of viewing trust through the different lenses of goodwill, contractual, or competence can help people ask the right questions before making a decision about whether to let someone go or give them a second chance. Everyone is unique. To live an inclusive life, trusting people based on these shared levels of trust can promote diversity and a sense of community.

item.title: Family Issues Coming Up for the Holidays? What to Do
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Family Issues Coming Up for the Holidays? What to Do

Consider four of the classic family therapy theories as a guide.

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Family therapy theories can help guide our interactions with our family as we near the holidays.
  • Want to work on understanding your family history? Consider the work of Murray Bowen.
  • Interesting in changing the current interactions? Explore the work of Virginia Satir and Salvador Minuchin.
  • Stuck in an unproductive narrative with family members? Apply the forward thinking of Epston and White.

I know. You have booked your holiday vacation flights, train seats, or hotel rooms to lock in rates and are wondering how the hangout with family will go. Whether you are single or partnered, there may be tough emotional terrain for you, solo or together, to navigate. Next step? Consider what the classic family therapy theories have to offer.

Murray Bowen’s Family Systems Theory

In short, Bowen taught us that family patterns get handed down from one generation to the next. He believed that family members need to interact with each other with a combination of intellect and emotions, where intellect rules. In his eyes, members should not be overly emotionally reactive with each other and are asked to consider where they learned their patterns of interaction. A son who is strongly bonded with his father may be looking to be emotionally bonded to his own son to the exclusion of his daughters. A pattern is being repeated.

Drawing a genogram (a modified family tree) is one way to look at what is going on. In the genogram, look for connections that are fraught and see if you can free yourself from any unhealthy interactions. Be careful, though, as some family members may want more of a feeling response.

Virginia Satir’s Experiential Family Theory

Are you much more into feelings and clarifying communication? Satir is for you. She believed that anything can be talked about between family members: hurts, fears, hope, etc. Repressing feelings will increase anxiety and lower self-esteem. People should be able to express what they feel using “I” statements and then be able to hear and respond to the feedback in a non-defensive manner.

Clear communication, where the physical and verbal communication are aligned, is the goal. Be careful, though, because some families do not want open communication and may feel threatened by too much “stuff” being put out there.

Salvador Minuchin’s Structural Family Therapy

Finding yourself pulled into family conflict? A sibling and a parent are going at it, and you are jumping in between? Consider focusing on boundaries.

In this theory, a boundary should be around the different subsystems (parental subsystem and child subsystem), and crossing into another subsystem inappropriately is discouraged. You should not listen to a parent run down your sibling; that would be a boundary violation where you are being triangulated or caught between your sibling and parent.

Recognizing boundary crossing and triangulation and getting yourself out of sticky situations by refusing to participate is the goal. Be careful, though, as the forces pushing family members into each other may be unhappy with your extricating yourself.

David Epston and Michael White’s Narrative Therapy

Take time to ponder what the identity of your family is. Are you a chaotic family? A distancing one? Or a closely knit one that does not allow a lot of individuation?

Consider if you want to rewrite your own narrative or try to rewrite your family’s narrative. You may be seen as the big (or little) sister and always be treated that way; you can try to assume a more equal status in adulthood and not fulfill a role that fits a family narrative. Of note, if you are distant from your sibling(s), your children may think it is okay to be distant from each other.

Think about what you would like the relationships to look like and re-narrate where you want to go with your family. Be careful, though, as other family members may have different visions of the future.

Dealing With the Past, the Present, and the Future

These are bird’s-eye views of family therapy that need to be tailored for you and your family. Multiple readings and YouTube videos are available to dive more deeply into each of these theories. Depending on you, your approach can focus on the past (Bowen), the present (Satir and Minuchin), and/or the future (Epston and White). You can also have a dollop of each as you circle the family turkey before carving it up.

item.title: Living Without the Ability to Recognize Faces
item.description:
Prosopagnosia

Living Without the Ability to Recognize Faces

How prosopagnosia reveals subtleties of human perception.

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Prosopagnosia affects the ability to recognise familiar faces, even when vision is otherwise typical.
  • Face recognition varies across individuals, and can exist from childhood or develop following brain injury.
  • People with face blindness often rely on voices, clothing, and contextual information to recognise others.
  • Understanding face blindness reveals how much we take our own perceptual abilities for granted.

Imagine walking past a close friend in the street without recognizing them. Or meeting a colleague you have worked with for years and being unable to identify them until they start speaking. For most people, these situations might happen occasionally, particularly when someone appears in an unexpected place. For others, however, they are part of everyday life.

We often assume that recognizing faces is a relatively simple task. We see someone, recognize their features, and immediately connect their face to a name, memory, or relationship. Yet, this seemingly effortless process involves complex interactions between visual perception and memory.

For people with prosopagnosia, commonly known as face blindness, this process works differently.

What Is Face Blindness?

Prosopagnosia is a difficulty recognizing people's identities from their faces. The term originates from the Greek words prosopon (face) and agnosia (lack of recognition). Importantly, face blindness does not necessarily mean that someone cannot see a face or distinguish its individual features. A person might recognize someone's eyes, nose, or mouth but struggle to combine this information into a recognizable identity.

There are two broad forms of prosopagnosia. Acquired prosopagnosia can develop following brain injury, stroke, or neurological illness. Developmental prosopagnosia, on the other hand, is present from early life without an identifiable brain injury. Some people may therefore grow up without realizing that their ability to recognize faces differs from that of others.

Face blindness also varies considerably in severity. Some individuals struggle primarily with unfamiliar faces, while others have difficulty recognizing close friends, family members, or even their own reflection.

Interestingly, prosopagnosia may be more common than we once thought. Estimates of developmental prosopagnosia have often been reported at around 2 to 2.5 percent of the population. However, DeGutis and colleagues (2023), examining more than 3,000 participants, found that prevalence estimates varied substantially depending on the diagnostic criteria used. Their findings raise an interesting question about where we draw the boundary between unusually poor face recognition and face blindness.

Why Are Faces So Special to Our Brains?

Faces carry an extraordinary amount of social information. Within moments, we can often recognize a familiar person, interpret their emotional expression, and recall previous interactions. One explanation for our ability to recognize faces involves holistic processing. Rather than treating a face simply as a collection of separate features, we tend to process the relationships between those features as an integrated whole. This is partly why recognizing an upside-down face can be surprisingly difficult. Psychologists call this the face inversion effect: turning a face upside down disproportionately disrupts our ability to recognize it compared with many other objects.

Face recognition also involves a network of brain regions, including the fusiform face area, a region associated with the visual processing of faces. However, recognizing someone involves more than detecting their facial features. The brain must also connect what we see to stored information about that person's identity. Research on prosopagnosia demonstrates that these processes can become disrupted in different ways. Some individuals have difficulties constructing a stable representation of a face, while others can perceive facial features relatively accurately but struggle to connect them to a familiar identity. In other words, seeing a face and knowing whose face it is are not quite the same thing.

Recognizing People Without Recognizing Their Faces

One particularly interesting aspect of prosopagnosia is the strategies people develop to navigate everyday social situations. Someone who struggles to recognize faces might become especially attentive to a person's voice, hairstyle, clothing, posture, or distinctive movements. Context can also become important. Recognizing a colleague sitting in their usual office may be relatively straightforward, but encountering that same colleague unexpectedly in a supermarket could create considerable confusion.

Research by Portch and colleagues (2023) explored how people with developmental prosopagnosia sometimes recognize familiar faces despite their difficulties. Their findings highlight the importance of compensatory strategies and the ways people draw on additional information to identify others. These strategies can be effective, but they are not always reliable. Hairstyles change, people wear different clothes, and familiar individuals appear in unfamiliar places.

The social consequences can be significant. Forgetting someone's face might be interpreted as disinterest, rudeness, or a lack of attention. Yet, the difficulty is not necessarily related to how much someone cares about another person or remembers their previous interactions. A person may remember an entire conversation, someone's interests, and the details of their relationship, while still being unable to recognize that person's face.

What Face Blindness Reveals About Perception

Perhaps one of the most fascinating aspects of prosopagnosia is what it tells us about abilities we rarely question. Most of us do not consciously think about how we recognize a familiar face. The process happens so automatically that it becomes almost invisible. We only begin to appreciate its complexity when we encounter someone whose experience differs from our own.

Face blindness also challenges the assumption that visual perception is a single, unified ability. Someone can have otherwise typical eyesight, recognize objects, navigate familiar environments, and remember detailed information about people, while experiencing substantial difficulties with facial identity recognition. Like other perceptual differences, prosopagnosia reminds us that our experience of the world depends on how our brains organize and interpret information. There is also an important social lesson here. We often interpret people's behavior through the lens of our own abilities. When someone fails to acknowledge us, we may assume they are ignoring us. Rarely do we consider that they might simply not recognize us.

Understanding face blindness encourages us to question these assumptions and appreciate that even the most familiar aspects of human experience are not necessarily universal. Sometimes, the differences between our perceptual worlds are not visible in what we see, but in what we recognize.

item.title: Sowing the Seeds of Estrangement
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Sowing the Seeds of Estrangement

How the empty nest years can become a turning point between the generations

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Family estrangement usually develops over time rather than from a single event or interaction.
  • The transition to adulthood can make father–child relationships particularly vulnerable to conflict.
  • Unresolved disagreements can quickly escalate into painful relational ruptures between the generations.
Source: Karen282 / Pixabay

At this time, demographic data indicate that about 25 percent of the U.S. population is estranged from, or has cut ties with, a close relative at any one time, and 10 percent of the population is estranged from a parent or child in particular.

I do not know whether or not the number of these rifts is likely to rise or fall, and as far as I can tell, there is insufficient research when it comes to determining whether or not cutting off from a family member has psychological advantages or healing properties for one or more of the individuals who are involved.

What I do know is that family estrangement is tremendously painful for all parties and is sometimes accompanied by considerable emotional risks.

In my experience as a family psychologist, parent-adult child estrangement does not occur in a vacuum, nor is it usually the result of a single event or isolated interaction; it is better understood as the unfortunate outcome of a complicated relational history between generations.

I have also seen that estrangement exists on a spectrum—different individuals and families define it differently. It can range, for example, from chilly, superficial, or emotionally guarded contact to infrequent contact to a complete cessation of contact. One parent might experience a period of relative distance with an adult child as a natural and temporary (and possibly important) state, while another parent might experience this as a hostile, and potentially permanent, relational rupture.

One way or another, the empty nest stage is often when the seeds of a possible estrangement begin to be sown. And since I have been focusing on fathers in my recent posts, it is worth noting that, in my clinical experience, far more adults have experienced estrangement from their fathers than from their mothers.

With fathers in mind, here’s an example from my practice (names and some details have been changed to protect confidentiality):

Religion was a very important part of Robert’s life, and his involvement in church life was a priority for him and his wife, Arlene, as well as for his children. His eldest son, Andrew, a fine tennis player, joined the Fellowship of Christian Athletes, worked as a counselor at the church’s summer Bible camp, and eventually chose to attend a college with Jesuit roots and a strong Christian community.

During his first couple of years of college, Andrew became very involved in the campus ministry and said that he planned to be part of the university’s global mission for at least a year after graduating, a decision that was a source of great pride for Robert.

But by junior year, Andrew’s involvement in religious activities began to wane—he took a break from being a chapel worship leader and resigned his position as the chairperson for the school’s community prayer walks. When he was home on winter break, he informed his parents that he was no longer interested in pursuing mission work after he graduated. These changes became a growing source of friction between father and son, and frequent arguments about religious identity and commitment ensued.

As a result, Andrew began pulling away from his father, rarely responding to Robert’s texts, and often not returning his father’s phone calls for several days. When he did pick up the phone, his tone was cold, and his conversation was clipped.

A tipping point occurred during Andrew’s visit home on spring break when he declined to join his family for Sunday church services. Robert lost his temper and blasted Andrew, telling him that he was being an ungrateful son and an impious Christian. He angrily reminded Andrew that he was paying for his college with the goal that Andrew wouldn’t graduate with any debt, a reminder that Andrew heard as a threat to withdraw funding for his senior year.

Andrew indignantly retaliated against his father’s diatribe by prematurely ending his break and returning to college, vowing not to return home that summer and resume work at the church camp that had employed him since he was in high school. Instead, he coolly told his parents he would stay with a college friend near campus, find a job up there, and pay for senior year himself if he needed to.

So what began as a period of wary distance and verbal clashes during the second half of Andrew’s college matriculation quickly calcified into an acrimonious standoff that threatened to become permanent.

In future posts, we will examine the origins of estrangement more broadly and explore the specific forces driving alienation between father and son at this delicate, important developmental juncture.

item.title: A Cause of Repeating Harmful Relationships
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

A Cause of Repeating Harmful Relationships

Multiple hurtful relationships can indicate an untreated trauma history.

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Having many hurtful relationships can indicate a traumatic childhood event left untreated.
  • Capacity to feel fear and experience fight-or-flight is often replaced by freeze or detachment from feeling.
  • Coping strategies are distorted and can leave one vulnerable to another in a relationship.
  • EMDR is helpful for floating back to identify and process earlier trauma that impacts current functioning.
Source: Akbarnemati / Pixabay

Victims of intimate partner abuse (IPA) who find themselves repeating harmful relationships most likely have early life experiences that contribute to their vulnerability to perpetrators. Vulnerability does not in any way imply responsibility—that lies solely with the person perpetrating the abuse.

History of Trauma or Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs)

“Past exposure to abuse, neglect, or violence can shape a person’s coping skills, self-esteem, and learned understanding of what constitutes normal or acceptable behavior, increasing future vulnerability.” (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, March 2024)

What’s missing is the connection a child develops with his or her emotions that can then be distorted when a caretaker cannot help to identify, name, accept, tolerate, or regulate emotions (Mosquera, 2021).

During childhood, when unhealthy relational dynamics are present and repeated, there is a greater likelihood that those harmful experiences get internalized. When this occurs, both victims and perpetrators can be born. At an early age, some perpetrators learn to counterbalance through blaming others and the use of aggression, while victims might lean toward types of submission (Mosquera, 2021). These behaviors used in the service of self-protection can become well-established coping strategies that show up in future relationships.

Learned Behaviors Undermine Protecting Oneself

Victims of intimate partner abuse can have misguided coping strategies influenced by traumatic childhood experiences, such as neglect, emotional abuse, and physical violence, as well as cultural influences. The behaviors that victims learned early on to protect themselves and avoid the risk of harm can include obeying or pleasing others (e.g., fawning). Fawning means anticipating the needs and wishes of another to avoid conflict, danger, or rejection.

Trauma Responses of Fight, Flight, or Freeze

Victims with an untreated trauma history are often ill-prepared to notice red flags with a coercive intimate partner. Whether feeling entrapped in early life and/or with an abusive partner, they no longer experience the emotion of fear that elicits the fight-or-flight response. In both circumstances, it can’t be enacted. To experience the response of fear, we are sensing in our body an alert—something is happening that is unsavory or dangerous that needs our attention. Instead, the common response is freeze. To freeze is to detach from feeling, to be numb, as a way to cope and survive.

Treating Past Events That Can Feed Current Difficulties

In childhood, when no one assumes responsibility for mistreatment, the child experiences shame and believes that they are to blame. When you believe everything is your fault, you’re all the more vulnerable to an abusive intimate partner who uses blame, degradation, and violence or threats of violence.

For victims with a history of repeating the experience of harmful relationships, the past trauma becomes all the more necessary to address in treatment. At the same time, it’s critical to provide help to notice the use of freezing and use other tools to reduce or move out of it to be fully grounded. Trauma can’t be successfully processed when someone’s feelings are unavailable. In my experience of working with clients in trauma treatment, EMDR is one modality that has proven useful for floating back to find and treat those earlier adverse experiences that are impacting current difficulties.

To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: “The Forces” Is the Most Important Psychology Book of 2027
item.description:
Anxiety

“The Forces” Is the Most Important Psychology Book of 2027

This book lets an entire generation know that they are not alone.

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • The narrator’s journey is a tour through the absurd beliefs that organize ordinary life.
  • We all live inside stories so pervasive that we mistake them for the world.
  • Laura Vazquez hears, sees, and feels the world differently from you and me.
  • The narrator bathes the reader’s mind in the absurdity of every signifier.

“It is no measure of health to be well-adjusted to a profoundly sick society.” ~ Krishnamurti

“The Forces” by Laura Vazquez is a French novel that will be published in English next year. But it’s not really a novel or even a book: it’s a combination of a musical score and script for a five-part opera about existential psychology. Like “Finnegans Wake,” it is meant to be heard. And watching Ms. Vazquez’s readings of “Les Forces” on YouTube is like watching Gustavo Dudamel conduct Mahler: both Dudamel and Vazquez hear, see, and feel the world differently from you and me.

Ms. Vazquez is a fragile soul who sees through the veil of “normal” to reveal the organized madness of mundane existence more vividly than any Western philosopher. There are parts influenced by Wittgenstein’s aphorisms, and yet, they are sung. Imagine Charli XCX singing “The Tractatus.” This book is going to flabbergast a generation of readers the way “Generation X” and “Infinite Jest” rocked my generation. The diction and descriptions made me laugh and cry alternatively throughout.

For example, on page 2, the young narrator says, “I live in an apartment that is in a building that is in a city that is in a country, and I am not looking for trouble. If you saw me, you wouldn't notice me, because I'm not deformed or smelly and I don't raise my fists in the air while screaming in the streets, I haven’t stabbed anyone, I am polite, I stand up straight. My parents are normal people and they brought me up properly.” (my translation)

“Neti neti” in Sanskrit translates to “Not this, not that.” Artificial Intelligence calls it “contrast,” often first describing something in the negative, by what it is not. The narrator spends much of the book bathing the reader’s mind in the incomprehensibility of every convention in florid language that’s akin to a monkey wrench in our cognitive engine.

In my psychotherapy practice, Gen Z patients arrive overwhelmed by the world that Ms. Vazquez animates. They are intelligent, terrified, lonely, curious, furious, and suspicious that they have gotten the short end of humanity's stick. They were told to create a verisimilitude of their true selves that is marketable, collect credentials, demonstrate financial viability, work 24 hours per day in order to remain competitive, and then… maybe with a sprinkling of good luck and having chosen the right parents… the elusive goal of “happiness” will befall them.

Alas, they have done everything right, but who has time to be happy when reality is disintegrating all around them and their days as apex predators are numbered? They feel alienated, physically at risk by man-made (previously named “natural”) disasters, financially endangered, and unable to tell whether their anxiety and depression are a chemical imbalance, personal pathology, massive failure, unaligned chakras, childhood trauma, mood disorder, blistering disease, result of a borderline mother or narcissistic father, or a rational response to the society they were thrown into through no fault of their own.

“The Forces” will let them know that they are not alone.

Gen Z asks questions such as “What is a self when so much of it has been downloaded from family, social media, status anxiety, advertising, and trauma? What is real desire when every platform profits from manufacturing lack? What is a meaningful life when adulthood means joining a belief system that is bankrupt in every way?”

Previous generations relied on philosophers from Hegel to Heidegger to answer these questions, but many of these thinkers now seem both confused and confusing. Ms. Vazquez’s narrator shares the perspective of an alien anthropologist sent to Earth to report on human customs and rituals. Her primary insight is radical yet easily digested: reality is what we have narrated into normality.

“The Forces” proceeds in five “chants”: “Everyone Lies,” “Mystery and Truth,” “The House of the Dead,” “The Various United Sects,” and “The Earth Is Good.” The structure resembles a Bildungsroman, but for me, I see the perfect arc of the construction of a self, then its deconstruction, culminating in a rebirth.

In the first chant, the narrator perceives the discrepancy between authenticity and facades. She sees adults agreeing with consensus, reciting judgments about taste, and treating social compliance as reality itself. Pierre Bourdieu called this habitus; Jacques Lacan called it the Big Other. Vazquez allows us to experience it through the eyes of a child—a child who decries inauthenticity.

The second chant is set in a bar and introduces Claudie, who compels the narrator to confront the danger faced by every critic of conformity: the fantasy that these forces are escapable. The narrator sees other people as possessed by collective language, but as Jacques Derrida said: when you look up a word in a dictionary, all you find is other words.

The third chant is “The House of the Dead,” where the narrator encounters people addicted to substances, patterns, and—most memorably—sentences. This is a brilliant image for the ways people become addicted to their own rationalizations. As I tell my patients who accuse partners of acting irrationally, “Everything Adolf Hitler did was perfectly rational. To Adolf Hitler.” Addiction offers relief from the unbearable weight of reality, but that relief turns into a prison itself.

The fourth chant is called “The Various United Sects,” and the narrator enters a building filled with sects, each floor representing a more absurd dictum. Vazquez understands that secular people worship the gods of productivity, the therapeutic industrial complex, money, romance, politics, or the promise of technological salvation. We all live inside stories so pervasive that we mistake them for the world—that there is no alternative to capitalism, that adulthood means constant optimization, that desire is fulfilled through constant consumption, that social media is connection, and that self-worth depends on attaining someone else’s definition of “success." The narrator’s journey through the building of sects is a tour through the absurd beliefs that organize ordinary life.

The final chant, “The Earth Is Good,” gives the book its hard-won affirmative power. After the mall, bar, addicts, and sects, and the narrator enters nature. She finds meaning in mud, birds, and the strange grace of an environment before it is processed into words, brands, résumés, slogans, and propaganda. The narrator does not solve the world’s cruelty, abolish capitalism, cure loneliness, or transcend death. She discovers something more modest and perhaps more psychologically credible: creative expression, intimate attention, and reintegration with Gaia.

Gen Z does not find much solace in traditional existential psychology. They need a scintillating, vivacious, and enthralling opera that unveils the “forces” that have caused them to try to be well-adjusted to a sick society. “The Forces” performs that exegesis, exposing normality as insanity, and offering a poetically beautiful and peaceful path out of the Matrix. That is why this extraordinary novel/script/score/performance/poem will be the most important psychology book of 2027.

item.title: Stupidity Threatens Everything
item.description:
Education

Stupidity Threatens Everything

Personal Perspective: Why we must intelligently confront human stupidity.

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Stupidity is not simple ignorance.
  • Stupidity is primarily a problem of inspiration and motivation.
  • The intersection of unrelenting stupidity with serious global challenges may be unsustainable.

Will stupidity be the death of us? Could stupid people doing stupid things cripple or destroy civilization, maybe even cause our extinction? Is it possible? Likely? Inevitable? Suggesting that stupidity is an existential threat may seem ridiculous at first glance, but consider humankind’s current trajectory and ask yourself if this is sustainable. The combination of unrelenting stupidity with global threats and increasingly powerful new technologies may make a species-level catastrophe unavoidable.

Our brains are powerful engines of calculation and creativity. They are also fountains of stupidity.
Source: Guy P. Harrison

Today’s greatest perils—nuclear war, climate change, biodiversity loss, pandemics, ecosystem destruction, the possible rise of an artificial superintelligence—are all unnecessarily complicated and worsened by stupidity. Too many nations and corporations are led by people who haven’t bothered to understand these threats. Perhaps worse, some do understand them but choose to publicly ignore or deny them. Sadly, stupidity can be personally advantageous for some—at the world’s expense. Many news media owners, managers, and screen personalities promote objectively stupid positions on critical issues as a strategic business model to monetize, spread, and intensify mass stupidity. How long can this continue before humankind has a very bad day?

Apocalypse or not, stupidity is a constant drain and a danger of significant consequence. Fortunately, stupidity can be addressed and reduced, even if it may be impossible to eliminate. But first, what exactly is stupidity and why is it so common?

Once a medical term, “stupid” has been thoroughly popularized and weaponized in our everyday interactions. But this word is much more than a mere insult. Stupid does not mean uneducated or ignorant. Ignorance is an absence of knowledge, a condition remedied by learning. Stupidity, however, is a lack of desire and/or effort to acquire new and better information. Stupidity emerges from the stubborn resistance to learning and self-correction in light of new and better information.

Intelligence and education do not reliably protect us from stupidity. Gifted thinkers with advanced educational accomplishments can be profoundly stupid. Stupidity is not the inability to think. Stupidity is refusing to try.

Rejecting vaccines because you never learned the history of vaccines or how they work might be solved by a good book or the right conversation with the right person. Rejecting vaccines because you consciously chose to trust the rant of an unqualified podcaster over the evidence-based explanations of virologists and epidemiologists is an issue that simple education probably won’t solve.

Stupidity is unrestrained by national borders, economics, political philosophies, religions, ethnic categories, or anything else. It will not be solved by teaching lists of facts or giving everyone brain MRIs. Stupidity is best addressed as a problem of inspiration and motivation. Unfortunately, this means fixing stupid is an extremely difficult challenge. I taught enough science and history classes to know that explaining how the Apollo lunar landings happened or how Homo erectus made tools is easy. Lighting a fire in the mind of every student, keeping them curious and hungering for more, however, takes real effort.

We must confront a tough truth about the celebrated human brain. Stupidity is a normal and expected outcome. Our default settings make falling hard for misperceptions, mistakes, and lies routine. Stupid beliefs and behaviors flow naturally from the standard processes behind our daily perceptions and thoughts. The brain takes many error-prone shortcuts and constantly deceives us. We can’t justifiably condemn it for any of this because the brain evolved in prehistoric environments with survival as the overriding priority. But we can at least be somewhat aware of what’s going on in our own heads and decide to do our best to catch the more dangerous lies and delusions.

A crucial first step to reducing human stupidity is getting more people to understand that we all spend our lives inside a theater of the absurd, the carnival house of mirrors. Humility and caution are essential because the reality that we see, hear, feel, think about, and remember only vaguely resembles actual reality. When we look around, our brains create highly edited representations based on the input taken in by the eyes. Thinking clearly and rationally is never automatic or easy because our thoughts exist within a cloud of biases, emotions, and preexisting beliefs. We don’t remember our past exactly as we lived it. Instead, our brains tell us customized stories about the past. This is why critical thinking—the deliberate effort to evaluate evidence and carefully consider perceptions, thoughts, conclusions, and memories—is the nonnegotiable prerequisite to reducing mass stupidity.

As humans, we all suffer stupidity. The big question is how stupid we are willing to be collectively. Nobody promised existing would be easy. Extinction stalks every species. If we hope to continue sticking around, we must solve enormous problems in the coming years, decades, centuries, and millennia. Considering that our most serious challenges today are caused or exacerbated by stupidity, we had better start doing a better job of dealing with this issue. It starts with inspiring and motivating people—all people everywhere—to think well and think often.

item.title: When Family Gatherings Bring Back Old Wounds
item.description:
Family Dynamics

When Family Gatherings Bring Back Old Wounds

Preparing for difficult situations with others starts by understanding ourselves

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Family gatherings can revive old roles shaped by our early needs for belonging, recognition, and care.
  • Acknowledging and mourning unmet longings can ease the expectations we bring to family gatherings.
  • Preparation involves understanding our reactions and choosing how to engage, without trying to control others.

Family gatherings can bring us back to ways of being and relating that feel very old, far removed from our everyday lives. We may arrive feeling confident, capable, and secure, ready to navigate familiar yet turbulent waters, only to find ourselves repeating old patterns, such as seeking approval, becoming defensive, or struggling to speak.

Navigating difficult family relationships involves more than knowing what to say or how to enforce our personal boundaries. We also need to recognize how our own history shapes what we hear, what we expect, and who we become in those interactions. Therapy for relationship issues can help us understand why family encounters affect us so deeply, how some of those patterns are present in other areas of our life, and why they might be so hard to break.

As the holidays approach and you feel dread or anxiety creep in, “preparation” can begin with curiosity about these experiences. We cannot anticipate, let alone control, how others will behave, but we can become more aware of what we bring to the table.

Recognizing the Roles We Return To

Within a family system, whether a single parent with a single child or an extended family with numerous siblings, we take on specific roles. These roles may have been necessary to develop a sense of identity and belonging, or to secure attention and care from others.

For example, we may have become the dependable one who accommodates everyone else, the difficult one whose disagreement is dismissed or catered to, or the quiet one who appears to be “fine” even though their needs go unnoticed.

We may inhabit multiple roles, shifting depending on the circumstances, and they tend to persist long after childhood ends. These roles become central to how the family system operates, which is why we may feel a pull towards them. Sometimes our relatives continue to expect them of us; sometimes we resume them before anyone has asked.

These patterns and roles often developed around important emotional needs. For example, keeping everyone happy may have helped maintain closeness. Withdrawing may have protected us from humiliation or enmeshment. Becoming argumentative may have been the only way we felt we had to feel seen and heard. These responses carry with them a history and difficult feelings—anger, hurt, sadness, resentment—that we may not be aware of.

Hope, Longings, and Disappointments

Sometimes we arrive at family gatherings with hopes we have not acknowledged. Perhaps this time a parent will express recognition, approval, or pride, a sibling will try to repair an old injury, or everyone will feel close again. These are expressions of very old longings and emotional needs: the need to be seen, recognized, appreciated, and valued for who we are by those we love.

These hopes often remain unconscious, and we may actively deny them. Denying our own unfulfilled wishes and unmet needs might be preferred to experiencing the deep sadness and hurt those absences created. “Why would I want something that will never happen?” can be a defensive maneuver against the pain of mourning, as if the impossibility of repair undid the sense of loss.

These longings deserve recognition and compassion, regardless of whether they are likely to materialize. We also may need to surrender them, in order to avoid turning them into rigid expectations we place on others. This process isn’t easy because it usually involves grieving what we never had.

Family gatherings can confront us with these disappointments in ways that can be very painful. At the same time, when we approach them as tests to see if we are finally heard, respected, understood, taken seriously, or loved, ordinary disappointments and miscommunications can take on enormous significance. A distracted response from someone else, for example, may feel like confirmation that we have never mattered to them.

Preparation Starts Within

Before a family gathering, it might help to consider what has happened on previous occasions. What did you feel just before you became upset? Did you find yourself trying to keep everyone happy? Did you withdraw, feel defensive, or look for someone to take your side? Were you giving cues about something you wanted without asking directly? These questions might shed some light on the roles and hopes that may have been at stake.

Younger parts of ourselves will inevitably make an appearance at family gatherings. This can be comforting, as when we feel attended to and cared for by someone who knows us well, but also hurtful, anxiety-provoking, or enraging when we anticipate judgment, punishment, rejection, or humiliation. The aim is not to judge any of our reactions, but to recognize them early enough so that we may have some choice about what to do next.

Recognizing the inevitable interaction between past and present when you are with your family does not mean dismissing your perceptions or excusing mistreatment. But it can help you distinguish what is happening now from what you may have learned to anticipate. It can allow you to create a space between the past and the present, leaving room to behave and respond in ways that don’t feel like repetitions of old patterns.

Preparing emotionally also involves acknowledging any unfulfilled longings and wishes you might harbor, while at the same time considering what other people are realistically able to offer. Insisting on getting something you deeply need from someone unable to provide it is one of the most difficult things to experience—and yet growth will likely require us to surrender those demands. Recognizing these limitations may bring up difficult feelings of grief and sadness, but mourning can loosen the pressure we placed on others.

In addition to asking yourself what you hope from others, it is helpful to consider how you want to show up. Perhaps you want to speak more honestly, try to remain curious instead of being defensive, stop assuming responsibility for others’ enjoyment, or attempt to be more generous with your attention. An intention is no guarantee that things will be different, but it can enhance your sense of agency and direction.

You can also think ahead about how to confront difficult moments you can anticipate, such as responding to uncomfortable questions or hurtful comments, or setting boundaries if a conversation becomes heated. Boundaries are not about dictating other people’s behaviors, but about thinking in advance about how you want to engage.

Finally, preparation might involve deciding whether a shorter visit or no visit at all is appropriate. Most people will have multiple feelings about an upcoming family gathering when things have felt tense in the past: guilty for not wanting to go, obligated to attend, or excited to see specific people. We need to make space for the complexity of our emotions and try to balance them within ourselves.

Family dynamics can be difficult to recognize because they shaped our personality, our expectations of others, and how we experience ourselves. The goal of “preparation” is not to avoid discomfort or disappointment, since those are natural feelings in most close and long-standing relationships. Making sure everything goes peacefully and that everyone gets along is also an unrealistic goal to put on one person’s shoulders. What can be within reach is to acknowledge and accept the feelings, expectations, and hopes you are bringing within yourself, mourn unmet longings and unfulfilled wishes, consider how you want to engage with others, and set intentions for how you would like to show up.
